title: Organic azide
wikitext:
{{short description|Organic compounds containing the azide (N3) functional group}}
[[File:Organic azide resonance.svg|thumb|The azide functional group can be shown by two resonance structures.]]
An '''organic azide''' is an [[organic compound]] that contains an azide (–{{chem2|N3}}) [[functional group]].<ref name = braese/> Because of the hazards associated with their use, few azides are used commercially although they exhibit interesting reactivity for researchers. Low [[molecular mass|molecular weight]] azides are considered especially hazardous and are avoided. In the research laboratory, azides are precursors to [[amine]]s. They are also popular for their participation in the "[[click reaction]]" between an azide and an alkyne and in [[Staudinger ligation]]. These two reactions are generally quite reliable, lending themselves to [[combinatorial chemistry]].

== History ==
[[Phenyl azide]] ("diazoamidobenzol"), was prepared in 1864 by [[Peter Griess]] by the reaction of ammonia and [[phenyldiazonium]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Griess|first1=John Peter|last2=Hofmann|first2=August Wilhelm Von|date=1864-01-01|title=XX. On a new class of compounds in which nitrogen is substituted for hydrogen|journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London|volume=13|pages=375–384|doi=10.1098/rspl.1863.0082|s2cid=94746575|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Griess|first=Peter|date=1866|title=Ueber eine neue Klasse organischer Verbindungen, in denen Wasserstoff durch Stickstoff vertreten ist|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jlac.18661370105|journal=Annalen der Chemie und Pharmacie|language=de|volume=137|issue=1|pages=39–91|doi=10.1002/jlac.18661370105|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In the 1890s, [[Theodor Curtius]], who had discovered [[hydrazoic acid]] ({{chem2|HN3}}), described the rearrangement of acyl azides to isocyanates subsequently named the [[Curtius rearrangement]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jay|first1=R.|last2=Curtius|first2=Th.|date=January 1894|title=Zur Reduction des Diazoessigesters|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cber.189402701151|journal=Berichte der Deutschen Chemischen Gesellschaft|language=de|volume=27|issue=1|pages=775–778|doi=10.1002/cber.189402701151}}</ref> [[Rolf Huisgen]] described the eponymous [[1,3-dipolar cycloaddition]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Huisgen|first=Rolf|date=October 1963|title=1,3-Dipolar Cycloadditions. Past and Future|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.196305651|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English|language=en|volume=2|issue=10|pages=565–598|doi=10.1002/anie.196305651|issn=0570-0833|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Huisgen|first=R.|date=November 1963|title=Kinetics and Mechanism of 1,3-Dipolr Cycloadditions|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anie.196306331|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English|language=en|volume=2|issue=11|pages=633–645|doi=10.1002/anie.196306331|issn=0570-0833|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The interest in azides among organic chemists has been relatively modest due to the reported [[instability]] of these compounds.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book|title=Organic azides: syntheses and applications|date=2010|publisher=John Wiley|others=Stefan Bräse, Klaus Banert|isbn=978-0-470-68252-4|location=Chichester, West Sussex, U.K.|oclc=587390490}}</ref> The situation has changed dramatically with the discovery by Sharpless et al. of Cu-catalysed (3+2)-cycloadditions between organic azides and terminal alkynes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Demko|first1=Zachary P.|last2=Sharpless|first2=K. Barry|date=November 2001|title=Preparation of 5-Substituted 1 H -Tetrazoles from Nitriles in Water †|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/jo010635w|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|language=en|volume=66|issue=24|pages=7945–7950|doi=10.1021/jo010635w|pmid=11722189|issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kolb|first1=Hartmuth C.|last2=Finn|first2=M. G.|last3=Sharpless|first3=K. Barry|date=2001|title=Click Chemistry: Diverse Chemical Function from a Few Good Reactions|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition|language=en|volume=40|issue=11|pages=2004–2021|doi=10.1002/1521-3773(20010601)40:11<2004::AID-ANIE2004>3.0.CO;2-5|pmid=11433435|issn=1521-3773|doi-access=free}}</ref> The azido- and the alkyne groups are "[[Bioorthogonal chemistry|bioorthogonal]]", which means they do not interact with living systems, and at the same time they undergo an impressively fast and selective coupling. This type of formal 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition became the most famous example of so-called "[[click chemistry]]"<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Binder|first1=Wolfgang|last2=Kluger|first2=Christian|date=2006-09-01|title=Azide/Alkyne-"Click" Reactions: Applications in Material Science and Organic Synthesis|url=http://www.eurekaselect.com/openurl/content.php?genre=article&issn=1385-2728&volume=10&issue=14&spage=1791|journal=Current Organic Chemistry|language=en|volume=10|issue=14|pages=1791–1815|doi=10.2174/138527206778249838|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rostovtsev|first1=Vsevolod V.|last2=Green|first2=Luke G.|last3=Fokin|first3=Valery V.|last4=Sharpless|first4=K. Barry|date=2002|title=A Stepwise Huisgen Cycloaddition Process: Copper(I)-Catalyzed Regioselective "Ligation" of Azides and Terminal Alkynes|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/1521-3773%2820020715%2941%3A14%3C2596%3A%3AAID-ANIE2596%3E3.0.CO%3B2-4|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition|volume=41|issue=14|pages=2596–2599|doi=10.1002/1521-3773(20020715)41:14<2596::AID-ANIE2596>3.0.CO;2-4|pmid=12203546|issn=1521-3773|url-access=subscription}}</ref> (perhaps, the only one known to a non-specialist), and the field of organic azides exploded.

==Preparation==
[[File:PhN3bondDis&ang.svg|thumb|133px|Selected bond distances (picometers) and angles for [[phenyl azide]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/ol901122h|title=Controllable Selective Functionalization of a Cavitand via Solid State Photolysis of an Encapsulated Phenyl Azide|year=2009|last1=Wagner|first1=Gerald|last2=Arion|first2=Vladimir B.|last3=Brecker|first3=Lothar|last4=Krantz|first4=Carsten|last5=Mieusset|first5=Jean-Luc|last6=Brinker|first6=Udo H.|journal=Organic Letters|volume=11|issue=14|pages=3056–3058|pmid=19537769}}</ref>]]
Myriad methods exist, most often using preformed azide-containing reagent.
[[File:Overview_alkyl_azide_synthesis_Zhurakovskyi.svg|center|thumb|upright=2.5|Azide synthesis techniques.  Arrows represent [[retrosynthetic analysis|retrosynthetic]] steps.]]

===Alkyl azides===
====By halide displacement====
As a [[pseudohalide]], azide generally displaces many leaving group, e.g. {{chem2|Br−}}, {{chem2|I−}}, {{chem2|[[Tosyl group|Ts]]O−}}, [[sulfonate]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Baran|first1=Phil S.|last2=Zografos|first2=Alexandros L.|last3=O'Malley|first3=Daniel P.|date=March 2004|title=Short Total Synthesis of (±)-Sceptrin|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ja049648s|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=126|issue=12|pages=3726–3727|doi=10.1021/ja049648s|pmid=15038721|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shaffer|first1=Karl J.|last2=Taylor|first2=Carol M.|date=2006-08-01|title=β-Glycosides of Hydroxyproline via an Umpolung Approach|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ol061424m|journal=Organic Letters|language=en|volume=8|issue=18|pages=3959–3962|doi=10.1021/ol061424m|pmid=16928048|issn=1523-7060|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and others to give the azido compound.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Righi|first1=Giuliana|last2=D'Achille|first2=Claudia|last3=Pescatore|first3=Giovanna|last4=Bonini|first4=Carlo|date=September 2003|title=New stereoselective synthesis of the peptidic aminopeptidase inhibitors bestatin, phebestin and probestin|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0040403903017994|journal=Tetrahedron Letters|language=en|volume=44|issue=37|pages=6999–7002|doi=10.1016/S0040-4039(03)01799-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The azide source is most often [[sodium azide]] ({{chem2|NaN3}}), although [[lithium azide]] ({{chem2|LiN3}}) has been demonstrated.

====From alcohols====
Aliphatic alcohols give azides via a variant of the [[Mitsunobu reaction]], with the use of [[hydrazoic acid]].<ref name = braese/> Hydrazines may also form azides by reaction with [[sodium nitrite]]:<ref name=OrgSynth >{{OrgSynth | title = Phenyl azide | author = R. O. Lindsay and C. F. H. Allen | volume = 22 | pages = 96 | year = 1942 | doi = 10.15227/orgsyn.022.0096}}</ref> [[Alcohol (chemistry)|Alcohol]]s can be converted into azides in one step using 2-azido-1,3-dimethylimidazolinium hexafluorophosphate (ADMP)<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kitamura|first1=Mitsuru|last2=Koga|first2=Tatsuya|last3=Yano|first3=Masakazu|last4=Okauchi|first4=Tatsuo|date=June 2012|title=Direct Synthesis of Organic Azides from Alcohols Using 2-Azido-1,3-dimethylimidazolinium Hexafluorophosphate|url=http://www.thieme-connect.de/DOI/DOI?10.1055/s-0031-1290958|journal=Synlett|language=en|volume=23|issue=9|pages=1335–1338|doi=10.1055/s-0031-1290958|issn=0936-5214|url-access=subscription}}</ref> or under [[Mitsunobu reaction|Mitsunobu conditions]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Sang-Hyeup|last2=Yoon|first2=Juyoung|last3=Chung|first3=Seung-Hwan|last4=Lee|first4=Yoon-Sik|date=March 2001|title=Efficient asymmetric synthesis of 2,3-diamino-3-phenylpropanoic acid derivatives|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0040402001000904|journal=Tetrahedron|language=en|volume=57|issue=11|pages=2139–2145|doi=10.1016/S0040-4020(01)00090-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref> with [[diphenylphosphoryl azide]] (DPPA).

====From epoxides and aziridines====
[[Trimethylsilyl azide]] {{chem2|(CH3)3SiN3}}, and [[tributyltin azide]] {{chem2|(CH3CH2CH2CH2)3SnN3}}, have all been used,<ref name=":02" /> including [[Enantioselective synthesis|enantioselective]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Martinez|first1=Luis E.|last2=Leighton|first2=James L.|last3=Carsten|first3=Douglas H.|last4=Jacobsen|first4=Eric N.|date=May 1995|title=Highly Enantioselective Ring Opening of Epoxides Catalyzed by (salen)Cr(III) Complexes|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00126a048|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=117|issue=21|pages=5897–5898|doi=10.1021/ja00126a048|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref> modifications of the reaction are also known. Aminoazides are accessible by the epoxide and aziridine ring cleavage, respectively.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sabitha|first1=Gowravaram|last2=Babu|first2=R. Satheesh|last3=Rajkumar|first3=M.|last4=Yadav|first4=J. S.|date=February 2002|title=Cerium(III) Chloride Promoted Highly Regioselective Ring Opening of Epoxides and Aziridines Using NaN 3 in Acetonitrile: A Facile Synthesis of 1,2-Azidoalcohols and 1,2-Azidoamines †|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ol016979q|journal=Organic Letters|language=en|volume=4|issue=3|pages=343–345|doi=10.1021/ol016979q|pmid=11820875|issn=1523-7060|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Saito|first1=Seiki|last2=Bunya|first2=Norio|last3=Inaba|first3=Masami|last4=Moriwake|first4=Toshio|last5=Torii|first5=Sigeru|date=January 1985|title=A facile cleavage of oxirane with hydrazoic acid in dmf A new route to chiral β-hydroxy-α-amino acids|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S004040390095024X|journal=Tetrahedron Letters|language=en|volume=26|issue=43|pages=5309–5312|doi=10.1016/S0040-4039(00)95024-X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

====From amines====
The [[diazo transfer|azo transfer]] compounds, [[trifluoromethanesulfonyl azide]] and [[imidazole-1-sulfonyl azide]], react with amines to give the corresponding azides. Diazo transfer onto amines using [[trifluoromethanesulfonyl azide]] ({{chem2|[[Trifluoromethylsulfonyl|Tf]]N3}}) and [[Tosyl azide]] ({{chem2|[[Tosyl group|Ts]]N3}}) has been reported.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Titz|first1=Alexander|last2=Radic|first2=Zorana|last3=Schwardt|first3=Oliver|last4=Ernst|first4=Beat|date=April 2006|title=A safe and convenient method for the preparation of triflyl azide, and its use in diazo transfer reactions to primary amines|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0040403906002450|journal=Tetrahedron Letters|language=en|volume=47|issue=14|pages=2383–2385|doi=10.1016/j.tetlet.2006.01.157|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

====Hydroazidation====
Hydroazidation of [[alkene]]s has been demonstrated<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Waser|first1=Jérôme|last2=Gaspar|first2=Boris|last3=Nambu|first3=Hisanori|last4=Carreira|first4=Erick M.|date=2006-09-01|title=Hydrazines and Azides via the Metal-Catalyzed Hydrohydrazination and Hydroazidation of Olefins|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja062355+|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=128|issue=35|pages=11693–11712|doi=10.1021/ja062355+|pmid=16939295|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Aryl azides===
[[Aryl]] azides may be prepared by [[Diazonium compound#Displacement of the N2 group|displacement]] of the appropriate [[diazonium salt]] with [[sodium azide]] or [[trimethylsilyl azide]]. [[Nucleophilic aromatic substitution]] is also possible, even with [[chlorides]]. [[Aniline|Anilines]] and [[aromatic]] [[hydrazines]] undergo [[diazotization]], as do [[alkyl]] [[amines]] and hydrazines.<ref name = braese>{{cite journal |author1=S. Bräse |author2=C. Gil |author3=K. Knepper |author4=V. Zimmermann | title = Organic Azides: An Exploding Diversity of a Unique Class of Compounds | journal = [[Angewandte Chemie International Edition]] | volume = 44 | issue = 33 | pages = 5188–5240 | doi = 10.1002/anie.200400657 | year = 2005 | pmid = 16100733}}</ref>
:{{chem2|[[Phenylhydrazine|PhNHNH2]] + [[Sodium nitrite|NaNO2]] → [[Phenyl azide|PhN3]] + NaOH + H2O}}

===Acyl azides===
{{main|acyl azide}}
Alkyl or aryl [[acyl chloride]]s react with [[sodium azide]] in aqueous solution to give [[acyl azide]]s,<ref>{{OrgSynth| prep=cv3p0846 | title = Undecyl isocyanate | author = C. F. H. Allen |author2=Alan Bell | collvol = 3 | collvolpages = 846}}</ref><ref>{{OrgSynth | prep = cv4p0715 | title = ''m''-Nitrobenzazide | author = Jon Munch-Petersen | year = 1963 | collvol = 4 | collvolpages = 715}}</ref> which give [[isocyanates]] in the [[Curtius rearrangement]].

:[[File:Preparation of acyl azides from acyl chlorides.png|300px]]

====Dutt–Wormall reaction====
A classic method for the synthesis of azides is the '''Dutt–Wormall reaction'''<ref>{{cite journal | title = CCXLI.—The action of diazo-salts on aromatic sulphonamides. Part I | author = Pavitra Kumar Dutt | author2 = Hugh Robinson Whitehead | author3 = Arthur Wormall | name-list-style = amp | journal = [[J. Chem. Soc., Trans.]] | doi = 10.1039/CT9211902088 | year = 1921 | volume = 119 | pages = 2088–2094| url = https://zenodo.org/record/1506564 }}</ref> in which a [[diazonium salt]] reacts with a [[sulfonamide (chemistry)|sulfonamide]] first to a diazoaminosulfinate and then on [[hydrolysis]] the azide and a [[sulfinic acid]].<ref>''Name Reactions: A Collection of Detailed Reaction Mechanisms'' by Jie Jack Li Published '''2003''' Springer {{ISBN|3-540-40203-9}}</ref>

:[[File:Dutt–Wormall reaction.svg|512x512px]]

==Reactions==
Organic azides engage in useful [[organic reaction]]s. The terminal nitrogen is mildly nucleophilic. Generally, nucleophiles attack the azide at the terminal nitrogen N<sub>γ</sub>, while electrophiles react at the internal atom N<sub>α</sub>.<ref name=":03">{{Cite book|title=Organic azides : syntheses and applications|date=2010|publisher=John Wiley|others=Stefan Bräse, Klaus Banert|isbn=978-0-470-68252-4|location=Chichester, West Sussex, U.K.|page=507|oclc=587390490}}</ref> Azides easily extrude diatomic [[nitrogen]], a tendency that is exploited in many reactions such as the Staudinger ligation or the [[Curtius rearrangement]].<ref name=Patai>{{cite book |editor=Saul Patai|doi=10.1002/9780470771266|title=The Azido Group|year=1971|series=PATAI'S Chemistry of Functional Groups|isbn=9780470771266}}</ref>

Azides may be reduced to [[amine]]s by [[hydrogenolysis]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.organic-chemistry.org/synthesis/N1H/reductionsazides.shtm|title=Amine synthesis by azide reduction}}</ref> or with a phosphine (e.g., [[triphenylphosphine]]) in the [[Staudinger reaction]]. This reaction allows azides to serve as protected -NH<sub>2</sub> synthons, as illustrated by the synthesis of [[1,1,1-Tris(aminomethyl)ethane|1,1,1-tris(aminomethyl)ethane]]:
:{{chem2|3 H2 + CH3C(CH2N3)3 → CH3C(CH2NH2)3 + 3 N2}}

In the [[azide alkyne Huisgen cycloaddition]], organic azides react as [[1,3-dipole]]s, reacting with [[alkyne]]s to give substituted [[1,2,3-triazole]]s.

Some azide reactions are shown in the following scheme. Probably the most famous is the reaction with [[phosphine]]s, which leads to iminophosphoranes 22; these can be hydrolysed into primary amines 23 (the [[Staudinger reaction]]),<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gololobov|first1=Yuri G.|last2=Kasukhin|first2=Leonid F.|date=February 1992|title=Recent advances in the staudinger reaction|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S004040200192229X|journal=Tetrahedron|language=en|volume=48|issue=8|pages=1353–1406|doi=10.1016/S0040-4020(01)92229-X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> react with carbonyl compounds to give imines 24 (the aza-Wittig reaction),<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Molina|first1=Pedro|last2=Vilaplana|first2=Maria Jesús|date=1994|title=Iminophosphoranes: Useful Building Blocks for the Preparation of Nitrogen-Containing Heterocycles|url=http://www.thieme-connect.de/DOI/DOI?10.1055/s-1994-25672|journal=Synthesis|language=en|volume=1994|issue=12|pages=1197–1218|doi=10.1055/s-1994-25672|s2cid=196726458 |issn=0039-7881|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fresneda|first1=Pilar M.|last2=Molina|first2=Pedro|date=2004|title=Application of Iminophosphorane-Based Methodologies for the Synthesis of Natural Products|url=http://www.thieme-connect.de/DOI/DOI?10.1055/s-2003-43338|journal=Synlett|volume=2004|language=en|issue=1|pages=1–17|doi=10.1055/s-2003-43338|issn=0936-5214|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Palacios|first1=Francisco|last2=Alonso|first2=Concepción|last3=Aparicio|first3=Domitila|last4=Rubiales|first4=Gloria|last5=de los Santos|first5=Jesús M.|date=January 2007|title=The aza-Wittig reaction: an efficient tool for the construction of carbon–nitrogen double bonds|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0040402006015158|journal=Tetrahedron|language=en|volume=63|issue=3|pages=523–575|doi=10.1016/j.tet.2006.09.048|url-access=subscription}}</ref> or undergo other transformations. Thermal decomposition of azides gives nitrenes, which participate in a variety of reactions; vinyl azides 19 decompose into 2H-azirines 20.<ref name=":03"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Álvares|first1=Yolanda S. P.|last2=Alves|first2=M. José|last3=Azoia|first3=Nuno G.|last4=Bickley|first4=Jamie F.|last5=Gilchrist|first5=Thomas L.|date=2002|title=Diastereoselective synthesis of aziridines from (1R)-10-(N,N-dialkylsulfamoyl)isobornyl 2H-azirine-3-carboxylates|url=http://xlink.rsc.org/?DOI=B202321K|journal=J. Chem. Soc., Perkin Trans. 1|language=en|issue=16|pages=1911–1919|doi=10.1039/B202321K|issn=1472-7781|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Alkyl azides with low nitrogen-content ((''n''C + ''n''O) / ''n''N ≥ 3) are relatively stable and decompose only above ca. 175 °C.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The chemistry of the azido group|date=1971|publisher=Interscience Publishers|others=Saul Patai|isbn=978-0-470-77126-6|location=London|page=626|oclc=501315944}}</ref>

Direct photochemical decomposition of alkyl azides leads almost exclusively to [[imine]]s (e.g. 25 and 26).<ref name=":03" /> It is proposed that the azide group is promoted to the singlet excited state and then undergoes concerted rearrangement without the intermediacy of nitrenes. The presence of triplet sensitisers, however, may change the reaction mechanism and result in the formation of triplet nitrenes. The latter were observed directly by [[ESR spectroscopy]] at −269 °C as well as inferred in some photolyses.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wasserman|first1=E.|last2=Smolinsky|first2=G.|last3=Yager|first3=W. A.|date=August 1964|title=Electron Spin Resonance of Alkyl Nitrenes|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja01069a049|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|language=en|volume=86|issue=15|pages=3166–3167|doi=10.1021/ja01069a049|issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Klima|first1=Rodney F|last2=Gudmundsdóttir|first2=Anna D|date=March 2004|title=Intermolecular triplet-sensitized photolysis of alkyl azides|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S101060300300368X|journal=Journal of Photochemistry and Photobiology A: Chemistry|language=en|volume=162|issue=2–3|pages=239–247|doi=10.1016/S1010-6030(03)00368-X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Triplet methyl nitrene is 31 kJ/mol more stable than its singlet form, and thus is most likely the ground state.<ref name=":03" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Travers|first1=Michael J.|last2=Cowles|first2=Daniel C.|last3=Clifford|first3=Eileen P.|last4=Ellison|first4=G. Barney|last5=Engelking|first5=Paul C.|date=1999-09-22|title=Photoelectron spectroscopy of the CH3N− ion|url=http://aip.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.479795|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|language=en|volume=111|issue=12|pages=5349–5360|doi=10.1063/1.479795|bibcode=1999JChPh.111.5349T |issn=0021-9606|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The (3+2)-cycloaddition of azides to double or triple bonds is one of the most utilised [[cycloaddition]]s in organic chemistry and affords [[triazoline]]s (e.g. 17) or [[triazole]]s, respectively.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Synthetic applications of 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition chemistry toward heterocycles and natural products|date=2003|publisher=Wiley|others=Albert Padwa, William H. ==Applications==
Some azides are valuable as [[bioorthogonal chemical reporters]], molecules that can be "clicked" to see the metabolic path it has taken ''inside'' a living system.

The antiviral drug [[zidovudine]] (AZT) contains an azido group.

extract: An organic azide is an organic compound that contains an azide (–N3) functional group. Because of the hazards associated with their use, few azides are used commercially although they exhibit interesting reactivity for researchers. Low molecular weight azides are considered especially hazardous and are avoided. In the research laboratory, azides are precursors to amines. They are also popular for their participation in the "click reaction" between an azide and an alkyne and in Staudinger ligation. These two reactions are generally quite reliable, lending themselves to combinatorial chemistry.
